case.name: A customer looks at everything for sale

rule.description:
It appears in the list of what is for sale with its own booking link, and it
is not described as an add-on there — because here, it is not one.
rule.name: An add-on sold on its own is listed like anything else

steps.text: a Chair sold with a Cover that can also be bought on its own
a customer looks at everything for sale
the Cover is offered with a link to its own page
the Cover is not called an add-on there
the Chair is still offered too
the Cover is still offered when booking the Chair

story.description:
Some things are only sold alongside something else — a seat cover with a
chair, a guide with a tour. An organiser can also mark one of those as
something people may buy on its own. It then gets its own page and its own
place in the list, and it is still offered with the thing it goes with.
story.name: An add-on that can also be bought on its own

rule.description:
The site shows the key the moment it is made, with a word to say it will
not be shown again. From then on the owner sees only the name they gave it.
Anyone who reads the list later learns what keys exist, and nothing they
could use.
rule.name: A key is shown once, and after that only its name

steps.text: the owner is looking at their keys
the owner makes a key called Shopfront
the owner is shown the key itself, and told to copy it now
the list of keys names Shopfront
the list of keys never shows the key itself

story.description:
An owner can hand a key to something that is not a person — their own
website, a spreadsheet, a booking screen in a shop — so it can read and
change what they sell without anybody signing in. The key stands in for the
owner, so it is shown once, kept by name afterwards, and can be taken back at
any moment.
story.name: An owner lets another system work on their behalf

case.name: The payment link for a part-paid 80.00 Retreat place

rule.description:
A reserved booking has a payment link the customer can open without
signing in. It names what they booked, what they have paid and what is
left, and offers to take the rest. It carries no personal details.

What happens after the offer is taken is a payment provider's business
and is not read here.
rule.name: The customer can see what is left

steps.text: a customer owes 80.00 for a Retreat place
they pay a deposit of 30.00
their payment link offers to take the 50.00 that is left
it names the Retreat place, 80.00 ordered and 30.00 paid
it says nothing about who booked

story.description:
Someone can pay part of what they owe now and the rest later. Until they
settle, the organiser must be able to see exactly what is still outstanding.
story.name: A customer pays a deposit and settles the rest later

case.name: A customer opens the booking page of an open bundle

rule.description:
A bundle that hides nothing tells the customer what they are getting
before they buy: the bundle's own name, and each thing inside it.
rule.name: An open bundle names what is inside it

steps.text: a Weekend group holding a Tent at 40.00 and a Breakfast at 10.00
the organiser sells the Weekend as a bundle, with the Tent at 25.00 and the Breakfast left blank
a customer opens the Weekend booking page
the booking page named the Weekend
the booking page named the Tent
the booking page named the Breakfast

story.description:
An organiser can take a group of things they sell and offer the whole group as
one bundle: a tent, a pitch and a breakfast sold together as a weekend. The
bundle sets its own price for each part, so a thing can cost less inside
the bundle than on its own. The organiser can also keep what is inside
private, and sell the bundle purely by its own name.
story.name: An organiser sells several things as one bundle

case.name: The listing's own record of the day shows the check-in

rule.description:
The organiser is told the name on the ticket and how many places it covers,
so they know how many people to wave through.
rule.name: A ticket for this listing lets the person in

steps.text: Alice has a ticket for the Ceilidh
the organiser reads Alice's ticket at the Ceilidh door
the Ceilidh's record of the day says Alice was checked in

story.description:
On the day, the organiser stands at the door with the listing's scanner open
and reads each person's ticket. The site tells them who is in front of them,
how many places that ticket covers, and whether to let them through. It also
keeps the people already inside off the list, so nobody is counted twice.
story.name: An organiser checks people in at the door

case.name: The organiser opens the record of someone who has booked before

rule.description:
The counts are shown as numbers they can edit, and the private note is shown
written out. Someone the site has never seen has a record of nothing.
rule.name: The organiser can read what is kept about someone

steps.text: the site has seen Sam book 5 times and get in touch 4 times
the organiser opens Sam's record
the record shows Sam booked 5 times through the site
the record shows 2 bookings the organiser added for Sam
the record shows Sam has visited 9 times
the record shows Sam has been in touch 4 times
the record shows the note about Sam written out

story.description:
The site keeps a little history for each person who deals with it: how many
times they booked, how often they have been in touch, and a private note only
the organiser sees. It is filed under a one-way code made from their email, so
the address itself is never stored. The organiser can read that record and put
it right whenever it is wrong.
story.name: An organiser reads and corrects the record kept about someone

case.name: A customer books a place on a group page

rule.description:
The customer keeps a ticket, and the organiser sees the person, their
contact details, and the answer they chose.
rule.name: A booking made on a group page reaches the organiser in full

steps.text: the organiser has a Summer Concert listing in the Summer Festival group that asks for a t-shirt size
a customer books one Summer Concert place and picks the Medium size
the customer can open a ticket for Summer Concert
the Summer Concert attendee list shows the customer, their email, and one place
the Summer Concert list download shows the customer picked Medium

story.description:
An organiser builds a listing, asks the customer a question, and shows the
listing on a group page. A customer books a place, keeps a ticket, and the
organiser sees the booking and the answer.
story.name: A customer books a listing the organiser set up

case.name: A customer pays 50.00 for a Workshop place

rule.description:
One sale and one payment, belonging to the same order. No booking fee is
taken unless the organiser has set one up.
rule.name: A paid booking is recorded once, and every page shows the same figure

steps.text: a customer paid 50.00 for a Workshop place
the Workshop earned 50.00 and the customer owes nothing
the booking holds one sale and one payment of 50.00, in one order
no booking fee was taken
every page shows the Workshop earning 50.00

story.description:
When someone pays for a place, the listing earns exactly what they paid, the
customer owes nothing, and every page that shows the figure agrees. The
booking is written down once — one sale and one payment, kept together.
story.name: An organiser sees what a paid booking earned

rule.description:
There is no separate step to publish. The owner writes it, and it is there
at the address they chose — for a visitor who was never signed in and never
will be.
rule.name: A page written is a page anybody can read

steps.text: the owner is writing the site's pages
the owner writes a page called Directions at "how-to-find-us"
the owner is told it saved
a visitor reading "how-to-find-us" is shown Directions

story.description:
Besides the things it sells, a site has pages that simply say something — how
to find us, what to bring, who we are. The owner writes those pages
themselves, chooses the web address each one lives at, and decides the order
they are offered in. A page is live as soon as it is written, so anyone can
read it straight away.
story.name: An owner writes the pages people read

case.name: A customer pays 80.00 for a place asking 30.00

rule.description:
Every place the organiser reads that figure shows the same amount, and the
customer owes nothing afterwards.
rule.name: The listing earns exactly what the customer chose to pay

steps.text: a Donate listing that asks 30.00 and lets people pay more
a customer chooses to pay 80.00
the Donate has earned 80.00
the customer owes nothing
the organiser sees 80.00 wherever the income is shown

story.description:
Some listings let a customer pay more than the price asked. What the listing
earns must be what they actually chose to pay, not the asking price.
story.name: A customer chooses to pay more than the asking price

case.name: The organiser switches back to a saved Stripe test setup

rule.description: Selecting a provider makes it active without removing its saved key.
rule.name: A saved test setup remains available after switching providers

steps.text: a Stripe test key is saved while Square takes payments
the organiser changes the payment provider to Stripe
the payment settings show Stripe selected with its saved key in test mode

story.description:
An organiser can switch between supported payment providers.
A saved provider setup remains available when selected again.
story.name: An organiser chooses a payment provider

case.name: Another customer takes the last place before confirmation

rule.description: The organiser can see the customer and the reason no place was booked.
rule.name: A paid customer who loses the place is kept and refunded once

steps.text: a paid listing became full while a customer paid
the late payment confirmation arrives
the late customer is kept without a quantity
the late payment is refunded once
the organiser can see why the booking failed

story.description:
A customer may finish payment after another customer takes the last place.
The customer must not be lost or charged without a clear outcome.
story.name: A paid booking loses the last available place

case.name: The organiser looks for someone who has not arrived

rule.description:
When a ticket cannot be read, the organiser can pick the person from a list.
That list holds only the people still to arrive, so nobody is let in twice
and a refunded ticket cannot be waved through by hand.
rule.name: Looking someone up by hand only offers people who are not in yet

steps.text: Alice has a ticket for the Ceilidh
the Ceilidh door offers Alice by name

story.description:
On the day, the organiser stands at the door with the listing's scanner open
and reads each person's ticket. The site tells them who is in front of them,
how many places that ticket covers, and whether to let them through. It also
keeps the people already inside off the list, so nobody is counted twice.
story.name: An organiser checks people in at the door

case.name: The organiser refunds a paid place

rule.description:
The listing stops counting the sale, the customer owes nothing, and the
money goes back where it came from.
rule.name: A refund hands back the money and undoes the sale

steps.text: a customer paid 45.00 for a Concert place
the organiser refunds the booking
the customer is handed back 45.00 once
the Concert has earned nothing and the customer owes nothing
the booking page says the booking is fully paid

story.description:
When an organiser refunds a booking, the customer gets back everything they
paid — the ticket, any booking fee, and any service charge. The organiser's
own figures must agree with the money that actually moved.
story.name: An organiser refunds a booking

case.name: The organiser creates a private studio floor hold

rule.description: The hold reserves capacity and never becomes a public listing or ticket.
rule.name: A service hold appears to the organiser but not to the customer

steps.text: Ceramics Studio Sessions is available for service work
the organiser creates a two-day Studio floor treatment hold for four places
the admin dashboard shows the Studio floor treatment hold
the public site does not show Studio floor treatment

story.description:
A service event reserves listing capacity without creating a customer ticket.
The organiser can see, duplicate, delete, and cost the hold.
story.name: An organiser holds and costs a service event

rule.description:
Pages are offered in the order the owner puts them, and they move them one
step at a time. Asking to move the top page up does nothing, rather than
failing or wrapping it round to the bottom.
rule.name: The owner decides what order the pages come in

steps.text: the owner has written pages called Directions, Parking and Opening
the owner moves Parking up
the pages are offered in the order Parking, Directions and Opening
Parking is already at the top

story.description:
Besides the things it sells, a site has pages that simply say something — how
to find us, what to bring, who we are. The owner writes those pages
themselves, chooses the web address each one lives at, and decides the order
they are offered in. A page is live as soon as it is written, so anyone can
read it straight away.
story.name: An owner writes the pages people read

case.name: The organiser looks at a listing booked three days at a time

rule.description:
The length shows on the listing's page for a listing booked by the day, so
the organiser can read it without opening the edit form. A listing not
booked by the day has no stay length to show.
rule.name: The listing's own page says how long its stays last

steps.text: a Lodge that is booked 3 days at a time, with room for 5 places a day
the organiser looks at the Lodge's page
the page says each booking lasts 3 days

story.description:
An organiser can change how many days each stay on a listing covers. The
listing's own page says how long its stays last. Stays already booked are
stretched or shortened to match a change, so the calendar and the bookings
never disagree — except where the customer chose the length themselves,
which is theirs to keep. A save that does not change the length leaves
every stay exactly as it was.
story.name: An organiser changes how long a stay lasts

case.name: Someone invited as an editor sets a password and logs in

rule.description:
The owner invites them by name and hands over a link. The editor chooses
their own password on that link, and from then on they log in and land on
the listings, which is where their work is.
rule.name: An editor sets up their own account from an invite

steps.text: the owner invites Sam to help with the listings
Sam follows the invite and chooses a password
Sam logs in
Sam is looking at the listings

story.description:
An owner can let somebody help with what the site says without letting them
near the people who have booked. That helper is an editor: they write and
change listings, groups and site pages, and that is the whole of it. They
are never shown a customer's details, what anything earned, or the settings
that run the site — and they hold no key that could open those details even
if they found a way to the page.
story.name: An owner gives someone the run of the listings, and nothing else

case.name: Sam signs up for the set-up shift

rule.description: The confirmation and attendee list show the shift the volunteer chose.
rule.name: A free shift sign-up appears on the organiser's attendee list

steps.text: Oakfield has three volunteer shifts with eight places each
Sam signs up for the set-up shift and asks for step-free access
Sam receives a free booking confirmation for the set-up shift
the organiser sees Sam and the access note on the set-up shift

story.description:
A volunteer can choose one shift and share an access need without paying.
The organiser can see the volunteer and their answer on the chosen shift.
story.name: A volunteer signs up for a free shift
